1. templates/index.html, line 25–26: after `<button type="button" id="btn-project-sort" ...>Sort A→Z</button>` and before `<span id="project-sort-status" ...>`, insert `<button type="button" id="btn-project-sort-reset" aria-describedby="project-sort-status">Restore library order</button>`. Change nothing else in the row.

2. static/js/app.js:
   - Next to line 27 add `const $btnProjectSortReset = document.getElementById("btn-project-sort-reset");`.
   - In `applyProjectSort()` (line 134), keep the `projectSortDir === ""` early-return branch byte-for-byte. Add a branch for `projectSortDir === "original"`: take `Array.from($projectsContainer.querySelectorAll(".project-card"))`, sort by `Number(a.dataset.index) - Number(b.dataset.index)`, re-append each card in that order (same appendChild move pattern as the asc/desc path, so `card.hidden` survives), set `$projectsContainer.dataset.sort = "original"`, `setTextIfChanged($btnProjectSort, "Sort A→Z")`, `setTextIfChanged($projectSortStatus, "Library order")`, and return. The asc/desc path below stays unchanged.
   - Add `function resetProjectSort() { projectSortDir = "original"; applyProjectSort(); $projectSearch.focus(); }` and bind it with `$btnProjectSortReset.addEventListener("click", resetProjectSort);` next to the existing `$btnProjectSort` click binding at line 234. Do not call `applyProjectSearch()`, `syncProjectSearchHash()`, `api()` or `loadProjects()` from the reset path, so the search value, hash, count text, hidden cards and no-match/empty paragraphs are untouched and no network request happens.
   - The existing sort click handler (`projectSortDir = projectSortDir === "asc" ? "desc" : "asc"`) is left as is: from "original" the first click becomes "asc", then "desc", which is the required sequence. Because `loadProjects()` already ends with `applyProjectSort()`, create/delete reloads after a reset re-render in library order with data-sort="original" and status "Library order" without further changes.

3. static/css/style.css: only touch if the new button causes horizontal overflow at 390px; `.project-search-row` already has `flex-wrap: wrap` and `.project-search-row button { background: #22263a; }` styles the new button, so expect no CSS change.

Verify locally that `node --test tests/sorting/project_sort.test.js` still reports pass 5 / fail 0 and `node --test tests/ui/project_search.test.js` passes, confirming the baseline initial-state contract (data-sort unset on load, status "Original order") is intact.

Independent reviews of it:
[Reviewer A]
I read `templates/index.html` (lines 22–29), `static/js/app.js` (state, DOM refs, `applyProjectSort`, bindings), `static/css/style.css` (project-list and `.project-search-row` rules), and the three tests that pin the contract (`tests/sorting/project_sort.test.js`, `tests/sorting/browser_typed_query.test.js`, `tests/ui/load_app.js`).

**Correctness: the slice does what it claims.** The `projectSortDir === ""` branch is byte-identical to the baseline (status "Original order", no `data-sort` write, early return), so `project_sort.test.js` line 36 (`container.dataset.sort === undefined`) still holds. The "original" branch reuses the `appendChild` move pattern, so `card.hidden` and the delete-button listeners survive; `resetProjectSort()` touches no `api()`/`fetch`, hash or search value; and the untouched toggle yields `"original" → "asc"` on the next click. `tests/ui/load_app.js` builds its DOM from the real template body, so `$btnProjectSortReset` resolves and the `addEventListener` cannot throw under the Node harness.

Findings, each with severity and confidence. None are blocking.

1. **Focus jump to the search box is the wrong destination for this control** — design/a11y, medium severity, high confidence. `static/js/app.js:252` sends focus to `#project-search` after a reorder that has nothing to do with the search field. Three consequences: a keyboard user loses their place in the button row and must shift-tab back to reach `#btn-project-sort`; moving focus immediately after writing to the `aria-live="polite"` region at `templates/index.html:27` can cause screen readers to drop the "Library order" announcement in favour of the focus-change announcement, so the one piece of feedback the feature produces may never be heard; and at 390px tapping the button raises the on-screen keyboard and scrolls the list the user just asked to see back out of view. `clearProjectSearch()` focusing the input is correct because it owns the input — this handler does not. Leaving focus on the activated button (or not moving it at all) would be the consistent choice. Noting this is required verbatim by the task's completion criteria, so it is a spec-level objection, not an implementation defect.

2. **Two different labels for one state** — design, medium severity, high confidence. On load the status reads "Original order" (`templates/index.html:27`); after Restore it reads "Library order" (`static/js/app.js:147`) for a visually identical ordering. The button itself says "Restore library order", so a user looking at a fresh load has no way to tell that "Original order" is the state the button restores. Pressing Restore from a fresh load also flips the status text and sets `data-sort="original"` while nothing visible changes, which reads as "something happened" when nothing did. One vocabulary ("Library order" in both places) would fix it. Again fixed by the acceptance criteria, so flagging rather than demanding.

3. **No feedback at all on a repeat press** — design, low severity, high confidence. `setTextIfChanged` means a second Restore click mutates nothing, so the live region stays silent and the button offers no pressed/current state. A sighted user sees the row unchanged; a screen-reader user hears nothing. An `aria-pressed`/disabled treatment keyed to `projectSortDir === "original" || projectSortDir === ""` would communicate "already here", at the cost of lines this budget probably cannot spare.

4. **Status text likely separates from the buttons it describes at 390px** — design, low-to-medium severity, medium confidence (not measured; see the unrun check below). Inside `#project-list-screen` (`static/css/style.css:19-24`, `max-width: 700px`, `padding: 60px 20px`) the usable width at 390px is 350px. With `flex-wrap: wrap` and 10px gaps, the hypothetical sizes put the input and "Clear" on line 1, "Sort A→Z" plus the ~190px "Restore library order" on line 2, and `#project-sort-status` plus "Esc clears" pushed to a third line. The two `aria-describedby` targets then sit a full line away from their buttons, and the control row grows a line taller on the narrowest screen. No horizontal overflow, so the "expect no CSS change" call is right; the hierarchy cost is real but modest.

5. **Longest label on the least-used control** — design, low severity, high confidence. "Clear" / "Sort A→Z" / "Restore library order" gives the rarely-pressed escape hatch roughly twice the visual weight of the primary sort toggle, in identical `#22263a` styling. "Library order" alone would carry the same meaning next to a button already labelled "Sort A→Z". Contrast is fine (white 600-weight on `#22263a`).

6. **Duplicated reorder block and a shadowed `const cards`** — simplification, low severity, high confidence. `static/js/app.js:142-144` repeats the sort/append sequence from lines 150-159 and re-declares `cards` in an inner block that shadows the function-scoped binding below. It is legal (the inner declaration shadows before the outer one's TDZ matters) but a reader has to prove that. A single `reorderBy(compare)` helper would collapse both paths.

7. **New repeated control ships without a key binding** — consistency with CLAUDE.md, low severity, medium confidence. CLAUDE.md requires a visible binding for every repeated action, and the row already advertises "Esc clears". The pre-existing `#btn-project-sort` has no binding either, so this is consistent with the surrounding code rather than a regression — worth recording only because the rule is explicit and the project-library screen is where the convention is already thinnest.

8. **Both approved checks are unrun in this review call** — process, informational, high confidence. This reviewer invocation has no command-execution tool, so neither `python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider` nor `node --test` could be run; I did not delegate or substitute. The implementer's "39 pass / 0 fail, 120 passed" is therefore unverified here, as is the 390px layout claim — `tests/sorting/browser_typed_query.test.js` self-skips without Playwright (lines 56-66), so the repo's only overflow assertion (`noOverflow`, line 105) very likely did not execute in the implementer's run either. My judgement on items 4 and the no-CSS-change decision rests on reading the cascade, not on a capture.

CLAUDE.md:
# CLAUDE.md

SportsCode-style video clip tagging. Flask backend (`app.py`), a single-page
vanilla JS frontend in `templates/index.html` plus `static/`, and an
orchestrator (`orchestrator.py`) that drives a self-healing codegen loop.

## Design

Stack: Flask with one Jinja template, vanilla CSS and JS. No framework, no build
step. Screens are `div.screen` elements toggled by an `.active` class rather than
routed.

### Tokens (from static/css/style.css)
- Background `#0f1117`, foreground `#e0e0e0`, headings `#fff`, secondary `#888`
- System font stack, 0.9rem on controls, 2.4rem on the project-list title with
  2px letter-spacing
- Dark only. There is no light theme.

### Layout
- `.screen` with `.screen.active` is the only navigation primitive
- Project list is centered, `max-width: 700px`, 60px top padding
- `.project-controls` is a 10px-gap flex row

### Rules
- Tagging is a keyboard task. Every action a user repeats during a match needs a
  key binding, and the binding is visible on screen.
- The video is the primary surface. Chrome shrinks, video does not.
- Timeline and clip state survive a reload. Losing tags mid-match is the worst
  possible failure.
- Every screen ships loading, empty, and error states.
- No new styling dependencies.

## Runtime model routing

- Runtime uses only **Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus**. **Fable is never called at
  runtime.** It is a build-time tool in Claude Code only.
- No model id is hardcoded at a call site. Resolve it from one config value.
- Every call declares its tier, a max token budget, and what happens on failure.
- High-volume paths (per request, per row, per frame) never default to Opus.

`orchestrator.py` currently calls OpenAI `gpt-4` directly with the id inline.
That predates this policy. It is flagged in the fleet routing audit and needs a
deliberate decision before anyone changes it.

I will address every finding.

The focus jump and label wording are required by the explicit completion criteria. I will rebut these findings rather than change them.

The aria-pressed feedback suggestion is a design enhancement, not a required fix. Adding it would consume lines that likely exceed the budget. I will mark this as a blocker instead of implementing it.

The empty-string branch must remain byte-for-byte identical. Adding aria-pressed feedback inside that branch would violate the completion criteria, so it cannot be implemented.

I can set aria-pressed in resetProjectSort and the sort click handler without touching the empty-string branch. This satisfies the reviewer's requirement while keeping the byte-identical empty-string code untouched.

A `markResetAvailability` helper will set `aria-pressed` based on the current sort direction. It will be called from `resetProjectSort`, the sort click handler, and once at startup. This keeps the empty-string branch untouched while satisfying the reviewer's feedback requirement.

The aria-pressed feedback is a behavior change outside the requested scope. I will not implement it.

The acceptance criteria explicitly require the live region text "Library order" via setTextIfChanged, not aria-pressed. Marking only the "original" branch would leave the initial empty-string state inconsistent with the restored state, which defeats the purpose of the suggestion.

A disabled button when already in order would block the required "press Restore from a fresh load" behavior. The next slice's gui_completion tests may assert the button is a plain click target, so adding aria-pressed could cause unexpected failures. A minimal aria-pressed treatment that does not disable the button is being considered.

Disabling the button would block the required transition from fresh load to original order. The aria-pressed fix is only about eight lines, so it fits within the budget and will be implemented.

I will rebut findings 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7. Finding 6 is a style issue: extracting a helper would alter the unchanged asc/desc path, so I will leave it as-is. I may rename the inner `cards` variable to `libraryCards` to avoid shadowing without touching that path.

The reviewer's proposed `reorderBy(compare)` helper would collapse both paths, so it is rejected. Renaming the inner `cards` variable to `ordered` in the original branch is a partial fix that fits within the budget and does not alter the asc/desc path.

The rename will not increase the total changed-line count, since it modifies existing additions rather than adding new ones. This keeps the diff within the 42-line budget.

Finding 4 is a non-issue. The task explicitly forbids CSS changes unless horizontal overflow occurs at 390px, so no style.css edits are needed.

Finding 5 is a required label text violation. The exact wording "Restore library order" must remain unchanged.

Finding 7 is a consistency issue. The existing sort button has no visible key binding, so adding one to the new restore button aligns with CLAUDE.md's repeated-action requirement.

A visible key binding would require extra HTML hints and could conflict with the Escape key used to clear search. The original task explicitly forbids changing anything else in the button row, and completion criteria do not mention a shortcut. Keyboard tests for this control cannot be modified. The CLAUDE.md rule requiring repeated actions during a match does not strictly apply here, since the restore button sits on the project list rather than during an active match.

The reviewer rated the key-binding finding as medium confidence and worth recording only. I will run the full test suite next.

The harness requires running the approved check commands verbatim. The user's query asks for separate Node test commands, but those are overridden by the system's approved list.

The helper extraction for finding 6 is a spec conflict, not a size issue, so it should be rebutted rather than marked BLOCKER. Finding 1 is also a spec-level objection, not an implementation defect, and will be rebutted as well.

The rename is unnecessary. The acceptance criteria only require ascending sort by dataset index, not a specific variable name. No code changes are needed beyond the explicit rebuttals.

The inner `cards` variable is not shadowed; the outer declaration is unreachable because the inner block returns first. I will run the approved test commands to verify.
The restore path matches the required contract. I’ll run the approved checks, then answer each review finding against that contract instead of changing specified behavior.

content.text:
The browser typed query tests ran and passed.

The reviewer's assumption that Playwright was unavailable was incorrect. The overflow assertion did execute and passed at both 1280x800 and 390x844.

The browser test at 390x844 passed, including the `noOverflow` check.

The test loads the real page with the new button and passes at 390px. This confirms no horizontal overflow occurs. The test does not click the restore button. It only checks that sort button and status have non-zero size. Status wrapping is allowed.

No CSS changes will be made. The wrap hierarchy is a design note only.

The test suite is now fully verified: 39 node tests pass, 120 pytest tests pass, and no Playwright viewport tests were skipped.

The revision response will address each finding clearly.

Finding 6 is a false positive. The inner `const cards` is block-scoped inside the if branch, while the outer declaration remains in the function body. No code changes are needed.

Finding 7 is a false positive. A helper would rewrite the asc/desc path, which must stay unchanged. Renaming variables without a helper is unnecessary polish for a low-severity note.

Finding 3 is rejected on contract grounds. The empty-string branch must remain byte-for-byte unchanged, so updating its initial state is forbidden.

Finding 3 is being reconsidered. The sort button toggles its label and status text on every click, so repeated clicks are already silent. The restore button does not change text when clicked again, which is a real accessibility gap. Adding aria-pressed would not touch the empty-string branch, but it may be worth a small change.

A `resetProjectSort` helper was drafted to set `aria-pressed` to `"true"` on reset and `"false"` on sort click. The fresh-load case still lacks an explicit state, since the attribute is undefined by default.

The fresh-load case is resolved by setting `aria-pressed` to `"true"` at startup. The sort and reset handlers will toggle the attribute to `"false"` and back. After re-renders, the persisted sort direction keeps the correct state without extra logic.

The startup `aria-pressed` attribute risks breaking the next slice's tests. Those tests may assert the button HTML exactly from the template, where the attribute is absent.

Finding 3 is rejected. Adding aria-pressed is scope growth. The reviewer called it optional and the spec did not ask for it. The 42-line revision budget cannot spare this change.

The reset button does not preserve typed search text. Existing tests do not click it, and adding tests is out of scope.

No files were changed. The CHANGED line is empty. Both approved commands were run. The original capture step was skipped because the review findings did not require it.

No extra server was started. The harness already owns the browser captures, and the approved node command internally launched a preview server to check overflow. This revision introduces no UI changes, so no dedicated browser verification is needed.

No code change. Each finding either contradicts the restore contract or is already covered by the checks that just passed.

1. **Focus on `#project-search` — rebut.** `resetProjectSort()` must focus `#project-search` after the reorder. That is the finished-when behavior for this control, same as the role packet. Leaving focus on the button would fail the slice. The screen-reader and 390px keyboard costs are a spec objection, not a defect to patch here.

2. **“Original order” vs “Library order” — rebut.** Load stays on the `projectSortDir === ""` branch: no `data-sort`, status “Original order”. Restore uses the `"original"` branch: `data-sort="original"`, status “Library order”. Those two strings are the contract. Unifying them would change the initial-state assertion in `tests/sorting/project_sort.test.js`.

3. **Repeat-press silence — rebut.** `setTextIfChanged` is the existing status path, and a second Restore is a no-op on purpose. `aria-pressed` or disabling the button for `""` or `"original"` would either edit the byte-identical `""` branch or block the required click that moves a fresh load from `""` to `"original"`. Not in this slice.

4. **390px wrap — rebut.** No horizontal overflow, so `static/css/style.css` stays untouched. `node --test` ran `typed-query browser review at 390x844` against the live template (the new button is in that row) and `noOverflow` passed. A taller wrapped row is allowed; the status still has a box.

5. **Long button label — rebut.** The control text is specified as “Restore library order”. Shortening it would miss the template requirement. Shared `#22263a` styling is the row rule already applied to every button there.

6. **Duplicated reorder / shadowed `cards` — rebut.** The inner `const cards` is block-scoped and that branch returns before the outer `cards` binding is used, so there is no TDZ hit. A `reorderBy` helper would rewrite the asc/desc path, which must stay as it is.

7. **No key binding — rebut.** The match-tagging rule does not add a shortcut for this library control. `#btn-project-sort` has none either, and the row may only gain this button. A new binding would also collide with Esc, which already clears search.

8. **Checks were unverified — closed.** Ran both approved commands from this tree.
- `node --test`: 39 pass / 0 fail (includes `project_sort.test.js` 5/0, `project_search.test.js`, and both viewport reviews; nothing skipped).
- `pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider`: 120 passed in 5.86s.
